claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has an established hierarchical heterostructured state.
Room-temperature tensile and fracture tests will be conducted at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
High-resolution DIC can measure spatially resolved local strain fields during the tests.
The measured DIC strain fields can be used directly to calibrate a simplified finite-element model.
Spatially resolved strain maps capture the effects of multilevel chemical fluctuations in the microstructure.
Spatially resolved strain maps capture the effects of phase boundaries in the microstructure.
Experimentally measured local strain heterogeneities constrain the finite-element model.
Constraining the finite-element model with local strain heterogeneities establishes a direct link between microstructural behavior and bulk mechanical properties.
The DIC-calibrated simplified finite-element approach bypasses the need for CALPHAD and first-principles simulations.
The method will predict Young's modulus within ±5% of direct experimental measurements.
The method will predict yield strength within ±5% of direct experimental measurements.
The method will predict toughness within ±10% of direct experimental measurements.
The method will reduce computational effort or simulation time by approximately 50% relative to conventional comprehensive multiscale approaches.
Insufficient DIC resolution would make the method unreliable when critical microstructural strain features cannot be resolved.
Changing temperature from the calibration condition may limit the finite-element model's predictive capability.
Changing strain rate from the calibration condition may limit the finite-element model's predictive capability.
A simplified DIC-calibrated finite-element model may not adequately capture complex fracture mechanisms.
